title: Linger and Lose: Knowledge Collapse in Low-Bit Language Models

paper.title: Linger and Lose: Knowledge Collapse in Low-Bit Language Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Training language models with ternary weights is commonly judged by loss and downstream accuracy, which record only a modest cost relative to full precision. We show that these metrics can conceal a much larger failure. We instead measure knowledge capacity, the factual bits stored per parameter, on synthetic biographies with known information content. We train GPT-2-style models from scratch with 2.5M to 50M parameters at five precisions. Under the standard cosine schedule, ternary models retain as little as 6% of an identically trained fp16 model’s capacity. The deficit widens with model size while perplexity rises by only 1.4 to 1.6 times. Measured throughout training, these models first acquire capacity and then lose most of it. We identify this knowledge collapse as a learning-rate dwell instability. Held near 1 1 – 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} with no decay, a pre-collapse model collapses within a few hundred exposures, and returning to a safe rate does not restore capacity. We then locate the collapse in the output head. It happens at a value the model can never predict. The weights there grow unchecked, while every other prediction the model makes is unchanged. We find that making the value predictable removes the collapse, regardless of which attribute carries it. A warmup-stable-decay schedule with a 10% cooldown increases ternary capacity by 2.7 times at 25M and 4.3 times at 50M. Gains are larger at lower precision. Cutting the output head’s learning rate prevents failure when training from scratch. The post-training quantization methods we tested recover no measurable capacity below 4 bits. Our findings suggest judging low-precision training by retained capacity during training rather than final loss.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Language models trained with ternary weights are usually judged by two metrics: how much the loss rises and how many benchmark points the model loses. Both can stay nearly unchanged while the model’s measured knowledge capacity falls by more than half. Allen-Zhu and Li (2024) showed that loss is a poor proxy for stored knowledge. They measured knowledge directly by training on synthetic biographies of known informational content and calculating learned bits per parameter. Their measurement covered only post-training quantization (PTQ), and they conjectured that quantization-aware training (QAT) would behave differently. We test that conjecture for precisions of int4 and below. Loss-based results imply that capacity degrades gradually as precision falls; we find instead that ternary models acquire capacity and then lose most of it to instability during training. We train GPT-2-style models from scratch at fp16, int8, int4, int3, and ternary precision, following Ma et al. (2024) , at four sizes from 2.5M to 50M parameters. We measure retention , the fraction of an identically trained fp16 model’s capacity that it retains, and find that int8 retains more than 90% of the fp16 capacity. Below int4, retention drops sharply, and under the standard cosine schedule, it falls further as the model grows from 0.36 at 2.5M to 0.06 at 50M. A representational limit would not predict this. As the number of people grows with the model, each person has the same parameter budget at every size, and a weight-precision limit would yield the same retention at every size. Previous work on ternary quantization evaluated through loss or accuracy ( Kaushal et al., 2025 ; Nielsen and Schneider-Kamp, 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) misses this because loss is insensitive to how much capacity the model loses. The model size dependence is driven by the knowledge load, which is the number of people N N that the model must learn, and not by the parameter count. Keeping N N fixed while the model grows removes that dependence (§ 4 ). The collapse appears only when N N grows with the model. Measuring capacity throughout training shows the load effect. At full load, ternary models at 25M and 50M first acquire capacity, then lose most of it before training ends. The failure is therefore not a capacity ceiling on ternary weights but training instability. We show that this collapse is a learning-rate dwell instability, and that in our experiments, the schedule, not the precision, decides whether it occurs. Contributions: 1. We measure knowledge capacity under quantization-aware training below int4, which prior work did not, and the PTQ methods we tested recover no measurable capacity below 4 bits (§ 4 , § 9 ). 2. We show that the size-dependent gap is a late-training capacity collapse driven by knowledge load rather than by parameter count. We identify it as a learning-rate dwell instability: a pre-collapse model held near 1 1 – 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} collapses without decay and does not recover at a safe rate (§ 5 , § 6 ). 3. We show, with nine dataset variants, that the collapse requires a value the model never learns to predict and that it is indifferent to which attribute carries that value and where it sits (§ 8 ). 4. We show that a warmup-stable-decay (WSD) schedule with a 10% cooldown removes the size-dependent decline in ternary retention and that slowing the output-head learning rate prevents the collapse from scratch (§ 7 , § 8 ).

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Knowledge capacity: Our capacity measurement follows Allen-Zhu and Li (2024) , who measured roughly 2 bits per parameter for GPT-2-style models on synthetic biographies. They showed a large drop under post-training GPTQ: int8 preserves capacity, while int4 loses more than half. They conjectured that QAT may be necessary for high-quality int4 models. We measure capacity under QAT itself, at int4 and below, and find that the deficit forms during training. A ternary weight can store at most log 2 ⁡ 3 ≈ 1.58 \log_{2}3\approx 1.58 bits, and none of the capacity we report approaches that value. Morris et al. (2025) provides a quantization-free capacity estimator, which we use as a cross-check (Appendix K ). Giorlandino et al. (2026) derives capacity thresholds for associative memories with continuous weights, and Gardner (1988) ; Gardner and Derrida (1988) ; Krauth and Mézard (1989) showed that restricting weights to a few discrete values lowers the maximum. Both results describe how much a model could store at most; our question is how much of what it has stored survives training. Low-bit training and its evaluation: Prior work on low-bit training is judged by loss or accuracy. Kumar et al. (2025) model quantized-training loss as a function of effective parameter count, and their fit predicts retention near 0.25 at 1.58 bits, close to our measurement under a short cooldown. That value needs a bias term they report only in an appendix, and 1.58 bits extrapolates below the 3 to 16 bits at which they pretrain. Ma et al. (2024) popularized ternary pretraining, and Spectra ( Kaushal et al., 2025 ) , Nielsen and Schneider-Kamp (2024) and ParetoQ ( Liu et al., 2025 ) evaluate it through loss or accuracy, reaching different verdicts on its cost. Our measurement observes a collapse that neither detects, which may explain the disagreement. Dettmers and Zettlemoyer (2023) found the total-bits-versus-accuracy trade-off turning against 3-bit inference, and our capacity measurement also turns. Duan (2026) show that perplexity can improve under quantization while interpretable features degrade, the same disagreement between loss and internal state that motivates our measurement. Schedules and optimizers in low-bit training: Existing work has studied each schedule and optimizer choice we vary, but through loss. Thomassen (2026) finds that 33% of the loss-optimal cooldown is across fp16, int8, and int6, and at int4, the choice is reported to be noise-dominated below 50M, our headline size. We test that fraction and find that loss and capacity disagree (§ 7 ). Xu et al. (2026) remove a convergence instability in 2-bit QAT with a progressive-precision curriculum, which we run against a control (§ 7 ). Nagel et al. (2022) show latent weights oscillating across quantizer thresholds, driven by the straight-through estimator’s gradient rather than by the learning rate. Our failure sits in the output head rather than the body and grows monotonically rather than oscillating. Wang et al. (2026) reports Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) outperforming Adam on tail-end associative memory; we use it only to locate where the collapse can be controlled and find no capacity advantage under a short cooldown (§ 8 ). A collapsed model that does not recover at a safe rate is closest to the loss of plasticity ( Dohare et al., 2024 ) . Late learning-rate dynamics and forgetting: Three recent papers precede us on the schedule. Catalan-Tatjer et al. (2026) show that post-training quantization error rises sharply once the learning rate decays, even as validation loss continues to improve. Watts et al. (2026) show that a shorter anneal, a higher peak rate, or sharpness-aware pretraining each leave a model less affected by later fine-tuning or 4-bit quantization. Rofin et al. (2026) tie decay-induced sharpening to forgetting under fine-tuning. All three pretrain in full precision and measure what survives a perturbation applied afterward. We add the same schedule dependence inside low-bit training, where capacity is lost while the model is still learning. Jagielski et al. (2023) found that memorized examples are forgotten the fastest just after a learning-rate decay step, at the post-decay rate, which depends on dwell time at the lower rate. In low-bit training, the same dependence appears as an abrupt collapse concentrated on one attribute rather than as gradual forgetting.

sections.heading: 3 Setup
sections.text: We vary precision, model size, and the learning-rate schedule, keeping the rest of the procedure the same (Appendix A ). Task and metric: We follow the bioS protocol of Allen-Zhu and Li (2024) . Each of N N synthetic people has six attributes (birth date, birth city, university, major, employer, gender) drawn from pools of known size and written out as short biographies. Birth date is composite, written as a month, day, and year drawn from 12, 28, and 200 values. Because we know the data’s information content, we can count the bits a model has learned from its loss. With p 1 p_{1} denoting the loss on a person’s name and p 2 p_{2} denoting the summed loss on the six attributes, both measured in nats, the capacity is R = N ⋅ ( max ⁡ ( 0 , log 2 ⁡ N 0 − p 1 ​ log 2 ​ e ) + max ⁡ ( 0 , log 2 ⁡ S 0 − p 2 ​ log 2 ​ e ) ) P , R=\frac{N\cdot\big(\max(0,\,\log_{2}N_{0}-p_{1}\log_{2}e)+\max(0,\,\log_{2}S_{0}-p_{2}\log_{2}e)\big)}{P}, (1) in bits per parameter. Here N 0 N_{0} is the number of possible names, S 0 S_{0} the number of possible attribute combinations, and P P the parameter count. Retention is R quant / R fp16 R_{\text{quant}}/R_{\text{fp16}} , where the fp16 model has the same size, data, and exposures, and always runs the standard cosine schedule. So changes in retention across schedules come from the quantized model alone. The max ⁡ ( 0 , ⋅ ) \max(0,\cdot) affects only collapsed cells, which we mark † \dagger and report under two other estimators (Appendix B ). Models and knowledge load: We train GPT-2-style decoders with rotary embeddings from scratch at four sizes (2.5M to 50M parameters) and five precisions: fp16, int8, int4, int3, and ternary ( Ma et al., 2024 ) . We call the transformer blocks the body . The embedding and the output head are quantized to int4 in every low-bit run, so “ternary” means a ternary body with an int4 embedding and output head. Only weights are quantized; activations stay in bf16. Following Allen-Zhu and Li (2024) , we give each model more knowledge than it can store. We set N N so the data hold 2.25 bits per parameter at every precision; we call this full load . Light load keeps N N fixed at 371k while the model size increases (§ 4 ); Appendix A lists the sizes and loads. Training and schedules: We train with AdamW at a peak learning rate of 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} for 1000 exposures , where one exposure presents every person’s facts once. Cosine decays from the peak to 10% of it; the low-bit work we compare against uses it, so we call it the standard schedule. Constant holds the peak rate throughout. WSD ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Hägele et al., 2024 ) holds the peak rate and then applies a cosine cooldown over the final fraction f f of training, with f = 0.1 f=0.1 unless stated. Evaluation and the collapse criterion: We evaluate capacity on a fixed subsample every 25 exposures and on the full corpus at the end of training, which gives the final R R . The capacity of a collapsed run flickers between low and partial levels across evaluations, so we define collapse over two of them. A run has collapsed when R R falls below 0.2 0.2 on two consecutive evaluations after exceeding 0.25 0.25 , with the first being its onset . A decline that does not meet this criterion is an erosion . Every collapse count in the paper uses this criterion, and each table states its seed counts.

sections.heading: 5 The Gap Is a Late-Training Collapse
sections.text: A final checkpoint cannot distinguish a model that never acquired capacity from one that acquired it and lost it. So we measure capacity throughout training. Under the standard cosine schedule, full-load 25M ternary runs rise toward the light-load level, peak, and then lose most of their capacity (Figure 2 , left). We also trained two seeds for 4000 exposures (4 × \times longer) and saw the same collapse, so longer training does not prevent it. At 50M, the collapse comes earlier: two of three seeds collapse a third of the way through the schedule, and the third collapses late. Figure 2: Continuous capacity traces, 25M ternary at full load, one line per run, against the fraction of each run’s schedule. Left : decaying schedules (cosine at 1 × 1\times and 4 × 4\times budget, cosine to a 30% floor). Right : constant LR, WSD with a 10% cooldown, and WSD at light load; the dotted line is the light-load reference. The collapse begins at the same fraction of the schedule, whether training lasts 1000 or 4000 exposures, so it follows the schedule and not the training time. Read as a learning rate, it begins between 1.0 1.0 and 1.6 × 10 − 4 1.6\times 10^{-4} in all five 25M configurations we traced (Appendix E ). Halving the batch size leaves that rate unchanged, which a gradient-noise account does not predict. The 50M seeds that collapse early do so at 3.8 × 10 − 4 3.8\times 10^{-4} , so the band belongs to the 25M model and is not constant across sizes. Holding the learning rate at its peak removes the collapse in all four constant-rate runs (Figure 2 , right). These runs cannot tell whether capacity is lost by decaying through this range or by dwelling in it; § 6 separates the two. The collapse is abrupt and narrowly localized: Birth date, the one compositional attribute, swings between storing several bits per person and being anti-predictive from one evaluation to the next. Birth city, university, and major stay steady across the same evaluations (Figure 13 ). Pooled over nine crashing runs, birth date stays above half its peak in 25–33% of post-peak checkpoints, and the three steady attributes in nearly all (Appendix L ). Employer and gender match birth date’s rate on a near-zero quantity, so survival does not order by cardinality. The same failure appears at full precision: One of three 50M fp16 seeds crashes at 70% of the schedule. Its name-prediction loss rises from 16 to 70 nats (Figure 13 , right, Appendix L ). Low precision, therefore, appears to lower the threshold of a failure it did not invent. Within a run, the training loss does rise at the crash by 0.14 0.14 – 0.19 0.19 nats, but the rise is small compared with the capacity lost. Loss misleads chiefly when you compare final losses across models, as Table 1 does. Where the increase sits: Scoring 16 archived 25M checkpoints per token position locates it precisely (Appendix G ). In all 11 collapsed checkpoints, the four steady attributes—the name and the birth day and year—sit within noise of their pre-collapse parents. The whole increase is on the birth month , which every ternary checkpoint predicts at chance, as does fp16 at both sizes; § 8 traces it to the output head.

sections.heading: 6 A Dwell-Dependent Hazard Window
sections.text: To distinguish collapse from decay at a learning rate, we branch the pre-collapse final checkpoints of two constant-LR runs to a fixed learning rate and hold them there. The parents end at R = 0.338 R=0.338 and 0.353 0.353 after 1000 exposures, and each branch keeps its parent’s optimizer state. We test nine learning rates from 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} down to 0.5 × 10 − 4 0.5\times 10^{-4} , two seeds at each, for 500 exposures (250 at the top rate); Table 2 lists the endpoints, and Appendix F lists the traces. Within a seed, every run starts from the same pre-collapse model, so the only variable is where it is parked. Onsets fall between 170 and 410 exposures, and nothing at or below 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} holds its starting capacity. LR decay doesn’t cause the collapse; time spent at these rates does. Outside the band, the hazard weakens but does not stop: Safety at 250 exposures does not mean safety at 500. Of the eight arms we held outside the band for the full 500 exposures, four collapsed, the earliest at exposure 360. At 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , a mild erosion by 250 exposures becomes a collapse in one of two seeds by 500. By 4 × 10 − 4 4\times 10^{-4} , the hazard is gone at this horizon, and the constant-LR arms hold the peak rate for the whole run. The map, therefore, measures a hazard rate that varies continuously with the learning rate and peaks near 1 1 – 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} (Figure 7 ). A fixed-length hold censors its tails, so the width we read off the map depends on how long we hold. Muon on the body, with AdamW on the embedding and output head, sees the same window. The onset band under cosine therefore reflects both how hazardous each learning rate is and how long the schedule spends there. Seeds change the timing, not the outcome: At the same held rate, seeds collapse at different times, one at 220 exposures and the other at 410 under 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} . Recovery is transient: of the 13 held-rate arms that fall below 0.2 0.2 after exceeding 0.25 0.25 , 12 climb back above 0.25 0.25 at least once, and none ends the hold there (Appendix F ). Collapsed traces do not settle but jump by a factor of three between evaluations, so we report onset under an operational definition rather than endpoints. A safe rate does not undo the collapse: We returned three collapsed checkpoints to the safe constant rate for 250 exposures. They average 0.13 0.13 to 0.16 0.16 over their last 50 exposures, well under their pre-collapse level. A fresh model at that rate reaches 0.27 0.27 in the same budget. Resetting the optimizer state, wholly or for either parameter group, separates no arm from replicate noise (Appendix F ). A collapsed model, therefore, does not regain its pre-collapse capacity at the rate that built it, a low-bit instance of loss of plasticity ( Dohare et al., 2024 ) . We bound that to the 250 exposures we tested, and our results suggest avoiding the collapse rather than repairing it. Any drop gives an immediate gain: We also found that every run that drops below 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , including those that later collapse, first jumps from about 0.34 0.34 to 0.40 0.40 – 0.49 0.49 within ten exposures and then erodes or collapses over the following hundreds. Lowering the learning rate raises capacity at once, and staying at the low rate then loses it slowly.

Running the whole precision row at 25M under both schedules (Table 3 ) shows two regimes on one curve. Below int4, the gain is recovery from the collapse. At int8 and int4, there is no collapse to recover, yet the gain is still positive: the milder cost a long decay imposes on a low-bit model, even when nothing dramatic is visible. We therefore read the schedule as acting on a single mechanism whose severity is set by bit-width, and all three fp16 WSD runs fall below the cosine mean. Three tests of the dwell account: Section 6 implies that the time spent in the hazard window determines where a schedule ends up. We check this on three schedules. (i) A 33% cooldown lands between the 10% cooldown and cosine, as its dwell predicts (Table 4 ). Thomassen (2026) identifies 33% as loss-optimal, so choosing a cooldown by loss does not account for knowledge; the divergence Watts et al. (2026) reports at full precision. One of three seeds collapses, so we claim the ordering rather than a dose–response. (ii) A 30% floor decays into the window and stays there. Two of three seeds collapse, and the third reaches the same final capacity, while two hold a pre-collapse level until late. What matters is accumulated exposure in the window, not whether the schedule is still decaying. (iii) A precision curriculum , fp16 → \to int8 → \to int4 → \to ternary with a re-warm at each stage, beats cosine but stays below WSD. A ternary model trained from scratch on the identical staged learning-rate path reproduces the plain-cosine result (Figure 5 ), so the benefit is the precision history, not the schedule. We take the recipe from Xu et al. (2026) and choose the stage fractions ourselves. Our results, therefore, favor the shorter of the two cooldowns we tested: 10% and 33%.

sections.heading: 8 Where Is the Control Point? Mechanism Triage
sections.text: Section 6 established when the collapse happens, not where it happens in the model or what is broken. This section asks both, and reports what we ruled out alongside what survived. The quantizer’s own statistics show nothing at onset: We logged how many body weights sit in each ternary state, how often they change state, and how large a typical update is against the quantizer’s level spacing (Appendix I ). None of them move at onset in any crashing run, and a WSD cooldown ends below the onset value of all three without collapsing. Because these statistics are aggregated across layers, they rule out a model-wide quantizer signature at collapse onset, but not a change confined to a particular layer. The output head diverges at the token the model never learns: The output head has one row per vocabulary token, and a row’s size bounds its logit. In one collapsing cosine run, the mean norm of the 12-month rows grows from 18.5 to 41.7, while the mean of the rest falls from 2.6 to 2.2 under weight decay. The growth begins at exposure 525, as the schedule enters the hazard window, and the largest month logit rises from 431 to 11,879 (Appendix G ). Month accuracy remains at chance throughout, so the growth reflects neither learning nor month loss. What prevents the collapse also prevents the growth: A 10% cooldown keeps the logits in the hundreds at every precision, and cutting the output head’s learning rate tenfold holds the month rows at 2.5 2.5 against the pre-collapse parent’s 18.6 18.6 . That cut also shrinks every other row of the head, so it limits the growth rather than selectively closing the gap between the month rows and the rest. We therefore read the collapse as unbounded growth of the head rows for a token whose gradient never vanishes (Appendix G ). The unlearned token causes the collapse, whichever attribute carries it: Nine corpus variants test whether the collapse needs a token whose loss never falls, each changing one property of the data and nothing else (Table 5 , Appendix H ). Removing the birth date stops the collapse; a control that re-sizes N N by the same amount but keeps the date does not. Removing only the month stops it, and so does making it predictable from the first name, where the model then learns it. Moving the date to the end of the biography changes nothing, so position is not the cause. Widening the month from 12 values to 200 stops the collapse outright and gives the highest 25M ternary capacity we have recorded under cosine. A representational limit would predict the opposite. Deleting the birth date and injecting one unrelated 12-way tag returns both seeds to the collapsed level, with the growth now on the tag. No variant we ran collapses without such a token, and injecting one restores it. With two seeds each, we claim the direction of every effect rather than its size. sections.heading: 10 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: Extreme low-bit training is unstable in ways current recipes were not designed to avoid. A representational limit would call for architecture research; a stability failure calls for schedule and optimizer research. Our results suggest two inexpensive changes: a short cooldown and a smaller learning rate for the output head. Our models top out at 50M parameters on synthetic biographies. Whether natural corpora contain values a model never learns is open, and we have not tested it. Even under WSD, ternary retention plateaus near a quarter of fp16, a residual gap we do not explain. On the one lineage we pre-registered, cutting the output head’s rate delayed the collapse rather than preventing it. The dwell map is at 25M only, and we tested reversibility over a 250-exposure horizon. One question we leave open: a collapsed checkpoint’s other predictions are unchanged, and a compression-based estimator reads no drop, so how much of the measured collapse is lost knowledge is unsettled. Ternary models’ reported robustness can reflect a metric blind to this failure rather than stable training. The collapse is a learning-rate dwell instability that a short cooldown removes. This work asks whether other low-bit failures are likewise schedule problems rather than capacity limits.

sections.heading: AI use statement:
sections.text: We used large language models as coding assistants throughout the process of writing and debugging training, evaluation, and analysis code, as well as for polishing and editing the manuscript. They did not generate results, fabricate citations, or decide which findings to report. Every number traces back to a logged run or a deterministic script, and the corresponding author verified every claim and number against the raw logs and takes full responsibility.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement:
sections.text: We specify the capacity metric, lattice, schedules, optimizer placements, and collapse criterion in § 3 . All numbers come from logged training runs (final-checkpoint and continuous capacity traces) and deterministic post-hoc scripts applied to trained checkpoints. We record seeds and hyperparameters for every configuration in the run logs. We will release the code, logs, and analysis scripts with the camera-ready version.

sections.heading: Ethics statement:
sections.text: This work uses only synthetic data. Each biography is procedurally generated and describes no real person, although the names, cities, and universities are drawn from pools of real ones. We train research-scale models of at most 50M parameters and release no deployed system.

sections.text: Every run elsewhere in the paper uses the clipped straight-through estimator. A reviewer of an earlier draft asked whether the collapse is an artifact of that choice. It is not, but the dependence runs in one direction only (Table 10 ). From scratch, the alternatives do not collapse: Neither the identity estimator nor stochastic rounding meets the criterion under cosine, on two seeds each. Both still gain from a cooldown, so the schedule ordering survives the estimator change. Slower learning does not explain the survival: stochastic rounding reaches R = 0.33 R=0.33 , the level from which every clipped cosine seed falls, and holds it to the end. The identity estimator peaks lower, at 0.27 0.27 , so for that arm we cannot separate the estimator from the state it never reaches. Once a clipped-trained model exists, the estimator stops mattering: We branch the pre-collapse clipped parents to a held rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} and run the hold with the identity backward pass. Both seeds collapse at onsets 275 and 245, within the noise of their clipped siblings. Identity-trained parents held the same way do not collapse and end above their parents. We therefore read the clipped estimator as building the state that collapses rather than driving the collapse itself, on two lineages. sections.heading: Appendix H Corpus Variants
sections.text: Each variant resizes N N so the corpus holds 2.25 bits per parameter (Table 14 ). Each adds vocabulary entries only while it is active, so the default vocabulary and P P remain unchanged. No birth date drops the attribute and stops scoring it. Three seeds reach R = 0.372 R=0.372 , 0.355 0.355 and 0.372 0.372 . Keep date drops university and major instead, resizing N N by about the same amount, and serves as the control for that resizing. No month renders the date without its month. Here max ⁡ | z | \max|z| on the date tokens stays between 78 and 202. Month from name sets the month to the index of the first name modulo 12. The month becomes a deterministic function of text the model already predicts. Date last moves the date sentence to the end of the biography and leaves its content unchanged. The birth city, now the first value in the text, is predicted at top-1 0.98 0.98 , while the divergence stays on the date. Month 200-way replaces the 12 month names with 200 tokens drawn uniformly. The model partly learns the wider month, reaching top-1 0.37 0.37 on the last date token. Inject tag drops the birth date and appends one sentence carrying a 12-way tag, a hash of the person’s name. The tag is deterministic given the name and carries no structure the model learns at this scale. It draws from its own generator, so it never consumes the shared population random state. Key–value corpus replaces biographies with six symbol-valued fields drawn from 256 options each, under four sentence templates. The lift does not depend on whether the variant collapses under cosine. The key–value corpus has no usable fp16 reference: Its fp16 cosine run rises to R = 0.241 R=0.241 by exposure 150 and then erodes to 0.109 0.109 , with code loss climbing from 30.5 30.5 to 32.5 32.5 nats. sections.heading: Appendix I Telemetry at the Collapse
sections.text: Body and interface co-adapt during training: A checkpoint-swap assay, without training, pairs one checkpoint’s transformer blocks with another’s embedding and output head. Branches held at high rates remain interchangeable with their parent; a branch held near the hazard window loses compatibility while retaining capacity; and a collapsed branch retains none (Table 16 ). Compatibility therefore fails before capacity does, so it is not sufficient for collapse. A capacity-landscape probe (Appendix M ) is consistent with a needle-like ternary basin but is only correlational. A tenfold cut of their learning rate alone does not recover; it differs from the recovered tenfold cell only in their weight decay, since AdamW decays as w ← w ⁡ ( 1 − η ​ λ ) w\leftarrow w(1-\eta\lambda) , so cutting η \eta alone also cuts the decay. Freezing them outright is worse than any rate cut, so these layers must keep adapting rather than merely moving less. sections.heading: Appendix J PTQ Method Details
sections.text: We implement GPTQ as block-sequential error compensation on our exact group-64 lattice (calibration Hessian, standard damping, Cholesky update, projection onto our integer or ternary lattice). At int8, it lands within 0.05 0.05 of the fp16 reference on our evaluator, which we can still reproduce from the archived sweep; the layer-wise reconstruction-error measurement we ran during development was not archived. AWQ follows the standard channel-scaling formulation with a per-layer grid search over the scaling exponent; NF4 uses the 16-level NormalFloat codebook at group-64. A calibration-source sensitivity check (held-out biographies, training text, random tokens) moved retention by less than 0.03 0.03 with the method ranking unchanged. Figure 12: Capacity by method and bit-width at 10M and 25M: QAT (green) against the PTQ methods (blue family). PTQ curves quantize seed 0 of each fp16 cell, so their int8 values track that seed; the QAT curve is the cell mean, as in Table 6 .

sections.heading: Appendix K Morris-Style Second Capacity Estimator
sections.text: The compression-gain estimator of Morris et al. (2025) (the difference in per-token compression between held-out and trained-on people, requiring no knowledge-token selection and no clamp) agrees with our primary metric at 10M (retention 0.235 0.235 versus 0.200 0.200 ) and sits above both clamp conventions at 25M ( 0.185 0.185 , against 0.090 0.090 and 0.126 0.126 ), consistent with the aggregate clamp undercounting a collapsed model’s residual knowledge (Appendix B ). fp16 measures 3.0 3.0 – 3.3 3.3 bits per parameter under it at 10M and 25M, and 2.5 2.5 – 2.7 2.7 at 50M, below the 3.5 3.5 – 3.8 3.8 range they report. Template-level knowledge is precision-insensitive at 9.4 9.4 – 9.9 9.9 bits per token across precisions, including ternary: the collapse is specific to facts about individuals. Scoring every checkpoint both ways, the two estimators agree up to a constant on pre-collapse models (Morris over ours is 1.53 1.53 – 1.71 × 1.71\times for pre-collapse ternary and 1.55 1.55 – 2.13 × 2.13\times for fp16) and diverge only on collapsed ones ( 3.6 3.6 – 5.3 × 5.3\times ). Because the estimator subtracts held-out people drawn from the same generator, template and grammar cancel, so the excess is person-specific information outside the six scored attributes; which estimator better captures retained factual knowledge cannot be settled without a token-level decomposition we have not run. Two cautions follow. It does not register the 25M collapse at all: collapsed cosine scores 0.567 0.567 against the pre-collapse constant-LR checkpoint’s 0.557 0.557 , so the 1.2 × 1.2\times WSD-over-cosine ratio it returns at 25M (Table 9 ) is measured on a quantity on which the effect is nearly absent. And our implementation caps the held-out cross-entropy at log ⁡ V \log V , since a trained model is anti-predictive on unseen people; that cap is what produces the negative 50M cell in Table 9 (uncapped, + 0.643 +0.643 against its sibling’s + 0.706 +0.706 ), so the entry is an artifact of the choice rather than a property of the checkpoint.

sections.heading: Appendix L Attribute-Level Structure of the Collapse
sections.text: Figure 13: Attribute-level view of the collapse. Left : per-attribute learned bits per person in one 25M ternary cosine run. Middle : birth date across four cosine seeds and a WSD control. Right : name-prediction loss of the crashed 50M fp16 seed. Pooling every post-peak checkpoint (89 to 179 samples across nine crashing full-load ternary runs) and marking an attribute as surviving if it sits at or above half its within-run peak, birth date survives only 25–33% of post-peak checkpoints, while birth city, university, and major survive essentially all. Employer and gender, which carry under a bit per person, survive at the same low rate as birth date (both 24%), a noisy ratio on a near-zero quantity; survival does not order by cardinality. The WSD-33% seed-0 final ( 0.259 0.259 ) is a real late capture, not an evaluation artifact: its subsample trace fell from 0.365 0.365 to 0.263 0.263 between exposures 975 and 1000, at a learning rate near 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} . At 50M, the name behaves as birth date does at 25M: the crashed fp16 seed and the int8 seed both end with negative learned bits there (Appendix G ), and the name is the only other attribute whose loss has an irreducible floor at ln ⁡ N \ln N .

Email: {ppaudel,ssheshap}@uwyo.edu Abstract Training language models with ternary weights is commonly judged by loss and downstream accuracy, which record only a modest cost relative to full precision. We show that these metrics can conceal a much larger failure. We instead measure knowledge capacity, the factual bits stored per parameter, on synthetic biographies with known information content. We train GPT-2-style models from scratch with 2.5M to 50M parameters at five precisions. Under the standard cosine schedule, ternary models retain as little as 6% of an identically trained fp16 model’s capacity. The deficit widens with model size while perplexity rises by only 1.4 to 1.6 times. Measured throughout training, these models first acquire capacity and then lose most of it. We identify this knowledge collapse as a learning-rate dwell instability. Held near 1 1 – 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} with no decay, a pre-collapse model collapses within a few hundred exposures, and returning to a safe rate does not restore capacity. We then locate the collapse in the output head. It happens at a value the model can never predict. The weights there grow unchecked, while every other prediction the model makes is unchanged. We find that making the value predictable removes the collapse, regardless of which attribute carries it. A warmup-stable-decay schedule with a 10% cooldown increases ternary capacity by 2.7 times at 25M and 4.3 times at 50M. Gains are larger at lower precision. Cutting the output head’s learning rate prevents failure when training from scratch. The post-training quantization methods we tested recover no measurable capacity below 4 bits. Our findings suggest judging low-precision training by retained capacity during training rather than final loss. 1 Introduction Language models trained with ternary weights are usually judged by two metrics: how much the loss rises and how many benchmark points the model loses. Both can stay nearly unchanged while the model’s measured knowledge capacity falls by more than half. Allen-Zhu and Li (2024) showed that loss is a poor proxy for stored knowledge. They measured knowledge directly by training on synthetic biographies of known informational content and calculating learned bits per parameter. Their measurement covered only post-training quantization (PTQ), and they conjectured that quantization-aware training (QAT) would behave differently. We test that conjecture for precisions of int4 and below. Loss-based results imply that capacity degrades gradually as precision falls; we find instead that ternary models acquire capacity and then lose most of it to instability during training. We train GPT-2-style models from scratch at fp16, int8, int4, int3, and ternary precision, following Ma et al. (2024) , at four sizes from 2.5M to 50M parameters. We measure retention , the fraction of an identically trained fp16 model’s capacity that it retains, and find that int8 retains more than 90% of the fp16 capacity. Below int4, retention drops sharply, and under the standard cosine schedule, it falls further as the model grows from 0.36 at 2.5M to 0.06 at 50M. A representational limit would not predict this. As the number of people grows with the model, each person has the same parameter budget at every size, and a weight-precision limit would yield the same retention at every size. Previous work on ternary quantization evaluated through loss or accuracy ( Kaushal et al., 2025 ; Nielsen and Schneider-Kamp, 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) misses this because loss is insensitive to how much capacity the model loses. The model size dependence is driven by the knowledge load, which is the number of people N N that the model must learn, and not by the parameter count. Keeping N N fixed while the model grows removes that dependence (§ 4 ). The collapse appears only when N N grows with the model. Measuring capacity throughout training shows the load effect. At full load, ternary models at 25M and 50M first acquire capacity, then lose most of it before training ends. The failure is therefore not a capacity ceiling on ternary weights but training instability. We show that this collapse is a learning-rate dwell instability, and that in our experiments, the schedule, not the precision, decides whether it occurs. Contributions: 1. We measure knowledge capacity under quantization-aware training below int4, which prior work did not, and the PTQ methods we tested recover no measurable capacity below 4 bits (§ 4 , § 9 ). 2. We show that the size-dependent gap is a late-training capacity collapse driven by knowledge load rather than by parameter count. We identify it as a learning-rate dwell instability: a pre-collapse model held near 1 1 – 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} collapses without decay and does not recover at a safe rate (§ 5 , § 6 ). 3. We show, with nine dataset variants, that the collapse requires a value the model never learns to predict and that it is indifferent to which attribute carries that value and where it sits (§ 8 ). 4. We show that a warmup-stable-decay (WSD) schedule with a 10% cooldown removes the size-dependent decline in ternary retention and that slowing the output-head learning rate prevents the collapse from scratch (§ 7 , § 8 ). 2 Related Work Knowledge capacity: Our capacity measurement follows Allen-Zhu and Li (2024) , who measured roughly 2 bits per parameter for GPT-2-style models on synthetic biographies. Mechanism Triage Section 6 established when the collapse happens, not where it happens in the model or what is broken. This section asks both, and reports what we ruled out alongside what survived. The quantizer’s own statistics show nothing at onset: We logged how many body weights sit in each ternary state, how often they change state, and how large a typical update is against the quantizer’s level spacing (Appendix I ). None of them move at onset in any crashing run, and a WSD cooldown ends below the onset value of all three without collapsing. Because these statistics are aggregated across layers, they rule out a model-wide quantizer signature at collapse onset, but not a change confined to a particular layer. The output head diverges at the token the model never learns: The output head has one row per vocabulary token, and a row’s size bounds its logit. In one collapsing cosine run, the mean norm of the 12-month rows grows from 18.5 to 41.7, while the mean of the rest falls from 2.6 to 2.2 under weight decay. The growth begins at exposure 525, as the schedule enters the hazard window, and the largest month logit rises from 431 to 11,879 (Appendix G ). Month accuracy remains at chance throughout, so the growth reflects neither learning nor month loss. What prevents the collapse also prevents the growth: A 10% cooldown keeps the logits in the hundreds at every precision, and cutting the output head’s learning rate tenfold holds the month rows at 2.5 2.5 against the pre-collapse parent’s 18.6 18.6 . That cut also shrinks every other row of the head, so it limits the growth rather than selectively closing the gap between the month rows and the rest. We therefore read the collapse as unbounded growth of the head rows for a token whose gradient never vanishes (Appendix G ). The unlearned token causes the collapse, whichever attribute carries it: Nine corpus variants test whether the collapse needs a token whose loss never falls, each changing one property of the data and nothing else (Table 5 , Appendix H ). Removing the birth date stops the collapse; a control that re-sizes N N by the same amount but keeps the date does not. Removing only the month stops it, and so does making it predictable from the first name, where the model then learns it. A representational limit would call for architecture research; a stability failure calls for schedule and optimizer research. Our results suggest two inexpensive changes: a short cooldown and a smaller learning rate for the output head. Our models top out at 50M parameters on synthetic biographies. Whether natural corpora contain values a model never learns is open, and we have not tested it. Even under WSD, ternary retention plateaus near a quarter of fp16, a residual gap we do not explain. On the one lineage we pre-registered, cutting the output head’s rate delayed the collapse rather than preventing it. The dwell map is at 25M only, and we tested reversibility over a 250-exposure horizon. One question we leave open: a collapsed checkpoint’s other predictions are unchanged, and a compression-based estimator reads no drop, so how much of the measured collapse is lost knowledge is unsettled. Ternary models’ reported robustness can reflect a metric blind to this failure rather than stable training. The collapse is a learning-rate dwell instability that a short cooldown removes. This work asks whether other low-bit failures are likewise schedule problems rather than capacity limits.
